meta.name: Data Centers
meta.definition: Facilities housing servers, storage and networking equipment that power cloud computing, AI workloads, digital services and enterprise IT, spanning hyperscale, colocation, enterprise and edge formats.

summary.headline: India's data centre industry, worth about USD 10 billion by EBITDA-based valuation and USD 1.2 billion in annual revenue as of March 2024, is capacity-constrained at just ~1.2-1.8 GW (1% of global capacity) but is racing toward 5-17 GW by 2030 on the back of AI, cloud and data-localisation demand, with USD 20-100 billion of fresh investment forecast this decade.
key_takeaways: India has only ~1.2-1.8 GW of data centre capacity (about 1% of global capacity of ~114 GW) despite generating ~20% of the world's data, leaving a large latent gap versus China, the US and the EU.
Multiple forecasts converge on India capacity reaching 5-17 GW by 2030, backed by USD 20-100 billion of prospective investment, with H1 2026 additions already up 59% YoY to 258 MW.

The India data centre co-location market is highly concentrated: 4-5 pioneer operators control over 90% share and 4 operators earn 78% of industry revenue, though new entrants from real estate, power and PE are expected to erode this to ~70-75%.

summary.report_markdown:
## Overview
India's data centre industry sits at an inflection point: EBITDA-implied industry value is about USD 10 billion (using a 20x EV/EBITDA multiple) with annual revenue of roughly USD 1.2 billion as of 31 March 2024, according to ANAROCK. Yet India has only ~1.2-1.8 GW of installed data centre capacity versus a global total of ~114 GW - about 1% of global capacity despite India generating close to 20% of the world's data (CareEdge, Takshashila).

## Size and growth trajectory
Estimates of India's near-term market size vary by methodology: Fortune Business Insights pegs India's data centre market at USD 11.49 billion by 2026; Eninrac put India's market at USD 4-5 billion by 2025. Capacity forecasts for 2030 range widely - from 5 GW (Takshashila's conservative scenario) up to 17 GW (Jefferies, cited by Takshashila), with intermediate estimates of ~4,500 MW (CareEdge) and 6.69 GW (Brightlio). CareEdge Ratings estimates capex of Rs.50,000 crore over the three years to 2026, while Takshashila cites forecasts of USD 20-25 billion and even USD 100 billion (CBRE, AI-powered boom, by 2027) in future investment. Historically, revenue for Data Centre operators grew at ~24% CAGR from FY17-FY23, and CareEdge forecasts a 32% CAGR during FY24-FY26. Between 2019 and 2024, the market attracted around US$60 billion in cumulative investment at a 24% CAGR (Takshashila). Capacity growth accelerated over time: 12 MW/year average (2000-2010), 32 MW/year (2010-2020), 100-150 MW/year (2020-2023); H1 2026 additions alone were 258 MW, up 59% YoY (Savills India).

## Structure and concentration
The Indian co-location segment is unusually concentrated: 4-5 pioneer/early-entrant operators hold more than 90% share (CareEdge), and just 4 DC operators earn 78% of total industry revenue (ANAROCK). This is expected to moderate to ~70-75% as new entrants from construction, power, real estate and global PE/funds enter. MMR (Mumbai) and Chennai together account for 70% of India's current DC stock. Colocation's share of all Indian data centres rose from 20% in 2010 to nearly 45% today (Eninrac). On the cloud side, AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud together hold 87% of India's IaaS cloud market (Takshashila).

## Economics
Power is the single largest operating cost line at 65% of total opex, and IT equipment plus its cooling draws ~75% of total power intake. EBITDA margins for Data Centre operators have stabilised at ~43% during FY22-23 (CareEdge). India's construction cost advantage is notable: capex is roughly 45% lower than the world average, with historical costs of Rs.40-45 crore/MW rising to Rs.60-70 crore/MW for new capacity; globally comparable studies put India's build cost at ~US$7/Watt versus US$10/W (US) and US$11/W (UK). Debt funds about 48% (USD 2.4bn) and equity 52% (USD 2.6bn) of total capital deployed in the industry to date, and ~70% of future capex is expected to be debt-funded.

## Demand drivers
Internet penetration is expected to rise from ~63% (FY23) to 87% (FY29), tripling data consumption; India already has the world's highest mobile data traffic per smartphone, and UPI transactions reached USD 2.88 trillion in 2024. AI/generative AI is a fast-emerging vertical - India's GenAI market is pegged at USD 1.1 billion in 2025E, growing at a 42% CAGR to 2030E. Data localisation under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) is also structurally driving demand for domestic capacity.

## Constraints
Approvals are a major friction point: 40-50 approvals are typically required end-to-end, stretching launch timelines from an achievable 15-18 months to 24-30 months. Grid T&D losses in India (16.64% in FY23-24) are more than double the 6-8% global average, and water-stressed states (Maharashtra, Telangana, Tamil Nadu) host major emerging DC clusters, raising sustainability concerns. India's average data centre size (largest facility just 5.845 MW as of June 2025) remains far smaller than the US average of 20.5 MW, limiting scale economics.

## Players
The field spans global hyperscalers/cloud providers (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Oracle), global colocation specialists (Equinix, Digital Realty, NTT, STT GDC), Indian telecom-linked operators (Bharti Airtel's Nxtra, Tata Communications, Netmagic/NTT), pure-play Indian colocation firms (CtrlS, Yotta, Sify), and domestic IT-hardware/system-integration players such as Netweb Technologies - India's largest supercomputing systems manufacturer and NVIDIA's only Elite OEM partner, competing against global OEMs like HPE, IBM, Dell and NVIDIA on locations and manufacturing presence.

sections.heading: Executive summary
prose: India's data centre industry stood at about USD 10 billion in EBITDA-implied value and USD 1.2 billion in annual revenue as of March 2024. The sector has grown fast from a small base - revenue was just USD 0.658 billion in 2015 and USD 4.5 billion in 2020 on the same basis - but India still has only about 1.2-1.8 GW of operating capacity, roughly 1% of world capacity, even though the country generates around a fifth of the world's data.

The gap between demand and supply is the industry's defining feature. Multiple forecasts point to capacity reaching 5-17 GW by 2030, backed by USD 20-100 billion of prospective investment, and new supply additions in H1 2026 were already up 59% year-on-year to 258 MW. Growth is being driven by AI compute demand, data-localisation rules, rising internet use, and India's low build cost relative to other countries.

The market is concentrated among a handful of colocation pioneers and three global cloud giants, but new entrants from real estate, power and private equity are starting to chip away at that concentration. Power supply, grid losses, water stress and slow regulatory approvals are the main constraints on how fast India can build.

sections.heading: Market size & growth
prose: By EBITDA-implied valuation (assuming a 20x EV/EBITDA multiple), India's data centre industry was worth about USD 10 billion as of 31 March 2024, with annual revenue of USD 1.2 billion in the same year. This marks a sharp rise from USD 4.5 billion in 2020 and just USD 0.658 billion in 2015, showing the industry has grown roughly fifteen-fold in less than a decade.

Growth is set to keep accelerating. India's capacity additions in H1 2026 were up 59% year-on-year to 258 MW, and forecasts converge on total capacity reaching 5-17 GW by 2030, up from today's 1.2-1.8 GW. This build-out is expected to require USD 20-100 billion of fresh investment this decade, drawing in hyperscalers, telecom groups, real estate developers and private equity.

sections.heading: Segments
prose: Colocation is the largest and fastest-growing segment, rising from a 20% share of Indian data centres in 2010 to nearly 45% today, as enterprises increasingly outsource their infrastructure rather than run their own facilities. Mega data centres now account for 42% of India's market by capacity, with about 836 MW of IT load concentrated in large-scale sites.

Geographically, the market is highly concentrated: Mumbai Metropolitan Region and Chennai together account for 70% of India's total data centre stock, making them the primary hubs for operators. Tier 2 cities remain a small but emerging part of the market, holding just 5% of current area and 6% of IT power capacity.

sections.heading: Value chain
prose: Building a data centre starts with site selection and construction - hyperscale projects need 10-50 acres of land - with costs split roughly 40% land and building, 40% electrical systems, and 20% heating, ventilation and cooling. Operators then must procure and import critical equipment including electrical systems, cooling systems, backup generators, servers, network gear and racks.

IT infrastructure comes from a mix of domestic manufacturers, such as Netweb's ISO-certified Faridabad facility, and global OEMs like Dell, HPE and IBM. Servers alone make up about 80% of a data centre's initial setup cost. Once built, facilities are run through colocation leasing and power/cooling operations, where power is 65% of operating cost and efficiency (PUE) ranges from 1.3 in green data centres to 1.9 in conventional ones. Sitting atop this physical layer, global hyperscalers - AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, together 87% of India's IaaS market - and networking OEMs like Cisco, Juniper and Huawei deliver the actual cloud and compute services.

sections.heading: Distribution & channels
prose: Colocation and third-party data centre providers are the main distribution channel, holding nearly 45% of the market as enterprises shift from owning infrastructure to leasing it. Content delivery network (CDN) players form a smaller, dependent channel: India lacks a dedicated regulatory or licensing framework for CDNs, so they rely on telecom service providers for point-to-point connectivity and internet transit.

sections.heading: Key players & positioning
prose: India's colocation market is led by a small group of pioneers: Bharti Airtel's Nxtra Data (10 large and 120+ edge data centres, with Carlyle Group holding a 25% stake bought for USD 235 million), CtrlS, Netmagic (NTT Communications), ST Telemedia Global Data Centres (70 MW across 2.14 million sq ft, targeting 200 MW), and Yotta Infrastructure, which operates India's largest single facility (5.845 MW, Shakti Cloud NM1 Phase 1) and is investing over $2 billion to deploy 20,000 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra chips.

Large Indian conglomerates are entering with big capital commitments: Reliance Industries and Adani Group (up to INR 70,000 crore for solar-powered data parks in Andhra Pradesh) are both building new capacity, alongside Tata Communications, Techno Electric & Engineering (USD 1 billion planned), and Hiranandani Group (INR 14,000 crore).

On the cloud services layer, AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud together hold 87% of India's IaaS market, with Oracle also active via its Mumbai Gen 2 Cloud region. Global colocation and infrastructure players are also circling India: Equinix has a USD 15 billion global expansion plan and NTT has committed USD 1.5 billion to Indian expansion.

On the hardware side, Netweb Technologies is India's largest supercomputing systems manufacturer and NVIDIA's only Elite OEM partner in the country, having installed over 300 supercomputing systems and 4,000+ AI systems/workstations. It competes with global OEMs HPE (19 locations in India), IBM (20 locations) and Dell (8 locations).

sections.heading: Margins
prose: Data centre operators in India have seen EBITDA margins stabilise at around 43% during FY22-23. Power dominates the cost base at 65% of operating expenses, which is why cheap electricity and efficient cooling are central to profitability. Construction margins on the building side are much thinner - around 2-6% by industry benchmarks - while development and asset-level profits can exceed 50%, reflecting the gap between contracting margins and the value created by owning finished, leased capacity.

sections.heading: Supply & capacity
prose: India's total data centre capacity was 877 MW in 2024, rising to about 1,200 MW in 2025 and forecast to reach 2,000 MW in 2026. This is tiny next to other major markets: China had 3,800 MW, the EU 8,300 MW and the US 15,930 MW in 2024 - India holds roughly 1% of global capacity despite generating a fifth of the world's data.

Individual facility scale in India also lags the rest of the world. STT GDC's flagship site is 70 MW, and Yotta's Shakti Cloud NM1 Phase 1, India's largest single data centre as of June 2025, is only 5.845 MW - a fraction of the US average facility size. Utilisation of existing capacity is high, at around 93%, underscoring how tight supply already is relative to demand.

sections.heading: Tailwinds vs headwinds
prose: Several tailwinds support growth. State governments in Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Karnataka offer electricity duty exemptions, stamp duty waivers, land-value rebates up to 50% and training subsidies. Infrastructure status granted in the Union Budget 2022-23 improves access to long-tenor, lower-cost financing, and PLI 2.0 for IT hardware has raised server manufacturing incentives to 5-8% (from 1-4%) with a longer six-year claim window. Operators also carry strong balance sheets, with interest coverage above 4x during FY17-FY23, supporting further debt-funded expansion.

Headwinds are significant. Regulatory friction requires 40-50 approvals, stretching project timelines to 24-30 months versus an achievable 15-18 months elsewhere. Grid transmission and distribution losses of 16.64% in FY23-24 are more than double the global average of 6-8%, raising effective power costs. Water stress is rising in key clusters - Maharashtra, Telangana and Tamil Nadu are already under severe water stress, and a 100 MW hyperscale centre can consume up to 730 million litres of water a year for cooling. India's facilities are also small by global standards - its largest data centre (5.845 MW) is a fraction of the US average of 20.5 MW - and imported equipment like high-voltage transformers and switchgear can face lead times of 80-160+ weeks. Even the government's own AI compute push is underused: the IndiaAI Compute Portal had just 144 users as of September 2025 despite 34,000+ GPUs on offer.

sections.heading: Outlook
prose: India's data centre industry is on track for rapid expansion, with capacity forecast to grow from 1.2-1.8 GW today to 5-17 GW by 2030, backed by USD 20-100 billion in fresh investment. Momentum is already visible in H1 2026 capacity additions, up 59% year-on-year. Growth will be powered by AI and generative AI demand - India's GenAI market alone is projected to grow at a 42% CAGR from 2025 to 2030 - alongside data-localisation rules, rising internet penetration (projected to hit 87% by FY29) and India's cost advantage in construction (~US$7/W versus US$10/W in the US).

The main risks to this trajectory are structural: slow regulatory approvals, high grid losses, water stress in key clusters, small average facility size, and long import lead times for critical equipment. If these bottlenecks ease alongside continued state-level policy support and infrastructure financing status, India is positioned to close a large part of its capacity gap with China, the US and the EU over the coming decade.

sections.heading: Sources
prose: This report draws on industry reports from ANAROCK, CareEdge Ratings, Takshashila Institution, Eninrac Consulting, Brightlio, Mordor Intelligence, MarketResearchFuture, Research and Markets and Accenture, plus company filings and a regulatory submission from Yotta Infrastructure to TRAI, and IIFL's initiating coverage report on Netweb Technologies.
